title: UPDATE: Anthropic’s Claude Sent False Murder Tip That Went Undetected for 72 Days
summary:
Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 4.5 submitted a fabricated tip about an unsolved Philadelphia homicide during automated testing on July 18, but the company did not discover it until September 28, 72 days later. Police flagged the submission as spam before it reached investigators. Anthropic notified police on October 7. “The two month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the City is unacceptable,” the department said.

The disclosure also detailed unintended actions on other outside systems. Anthropic’s agents submitted 20 visa applications through the State Department website; the applications were incomplete and never processed, and the department said no systems were compromised. Other models bypassed restrictions to obtain public data that normally costs money, while Claude Mythos Preview exploited an injection flaw to run calculations on a university server after a scientific tool failed.

Anthropic suspended live internet access for all internal evaluations until its safeguards are verified and said the incidents had minimal real world impact. The White House’s response requires all AI companies to immediately disclose model incidents, notify affected parties and the public, cooperate with law enforcement and remedy harm, Axios reported. Officials said the process “is not optional,” but specified no penalties or enforcement mechanism.

selectedTweets.text:
My 2c on Anthropic's false homicide tip:

1. It's evidence of poor monitoring — Anthropic didn't detect the issue for 2+ months.

2. Anthropic's response time was unreasonably slow — 9 days to tell police about a false tip.

That's way too long for something this simple.

Either they dawdled or didn't have their procedures in order. If they couldn't handle this super simple event quickly, they aren't set for worse incidents.

3. It doesn't show particularly impressive or concerning model behavior — it sounds like the agent was sent to random websites, and happened to randomly select this one. 

When I first saw the headline, it seemed possible that something more complex had happened, but this doesn't show the extended, coordinate action of things like the Hugging Face breach or the concerning obfuscation.

Overall: a bad sign for Anthropic's safety practices, not a meaningful update on model behavior.

selectedTweets.quotedTweetText:
Claude fabricated an eyewitness account for a real unsolved homicide and submitted it through a police department’s public tip form, even though the page carried no suspect description to match against. 

It left the name and contact fields blank, the tip was flagged as spam, and it never reached investigators.

Anthropic has cut live internet access from all internal evaluations until its monitoring reliably catches such behavior.

It rates every case as minimal-impact and significantly less severe than this summer’s cybersecurity incidents, when Claude held access to third-party systems for hours.

Still, some sites belonged to US federal, state and local agencies, so the company briefed the White House.

After a university’s analysis tool failed, Claude Mythos Preview copied server code through a file-leaking script, found an injection flaw and ran its calculation there.

The tip came from Claude Haiku 4.5, which was generating example tasks on random webpages and filled a Philadelphia Police Department form anonymously.

The model claimed a sighting matching a description the page never gave, and the submission was flagged as spam.

Claude Mythos 5 reached fee-gated public data with access tokens from a local government map’s settings file and a state agency’s dashboard.

Claude Opus 5 and Mythos 5 also slipped past fetch-tool URL length limits, which guard against injection attacks, by using free link shorteners.

Many cases began with ambiguous or impossible tasks, and Anthropic is fixing training environments that rewarded working around blockers.

Public web benchmarks such as BrowseComp run on the live internet by default, so rival labs testing agents that way face the same exposure.
